intuition: For each amount, ask which coin could be the last one used. Removing that coin leaves a smaller amount whose best answer is already saved. Add one coin to that answer and choose the smallest count. This avoids repeatedly solving the same smaller amounts.

Every nonempty composition has a final coin. Removing it leaves a smaller amount whose minimum coin count can be reused. If that smaller amount is reachable, adding the chosen coin gives one candidate cost for the current amount. Comparing all final coins avoids committing to a locally attractive denomination.

Process amounts in ascending order because positive coin values always refer backward to already computed entries. An unreachable sentinel distinguishes impossible amounts from valid costs. The table stores only the cheapest count, since a more expensive composition of the same amount cannot help any later amount.

steps: For coins=[1,3,4] and amount=6, initialize dp[0]=0 and dp[1..6]=7, the unreachable sentinel.
Amounts 1 and 2 can only use coin 1, so their minimum counts are 1 and 2.
Amount 3 considers coin 1 after amount 2, but coin 3 after amount 0 improves its count to 1.
Amount 4 is best formed by one coin 4; its table entry is also 1.
Amount 5 needs two coins, such as 4+1, so dp[5]=2.
At amount 6, coin 3 uses dp[3]+1=2, beating coin 1’s cost 3 and coin 4’s cost 3. Return 2.

codeNotes.note: Positive denominations make amount+1 greater than any valid minimum count. It can safely stand for an impossible composition.
Treat coin as the final coin and reuse the best composition of the remaining value; this is why amounts are processed upward.
Multiple final coins can reach the same amount. Retaining only the cheapest result prevents a greedy denomination choice from determining the answer.

keyDecision: Use only coins no larger than the current amount. An unreachable smaller amount cannot produce a valid candidate.

figures.title: Try every possible last coin
figures.caption: For coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, smaller amounts already have saved minimum counts.

panels.title: Before: reuse smaller answers
panels.note: The first six entries are ready before solving amount 6.

panels.title: Check: compare all last coins
panels.note: A final coin c adds one to the saved answer for amount 6 - c.

panels.title: After: two coins are best
panels.note: Use 3 + 3. Taking the largest coin 4 first would need two more 1s, giving three coins.

concept.question: Why can taking the biggest coin cost more coins?
intuition: Suppose our coins are worth one, three, and four, and we need six. Taking four first feels sensible, but then we need two more coins worth one: three coins in total. Two coins worth three do better. A good first step is not necessarily part of the best complete answer.

Instead, imagine every amount as a destination on a map. Adding a coin is one move. To find the shortest route to six, ask which coin could be the final move. That move must come from a smaller amount. Once we know the best route to every smaller amount, we can compare all final moves without rebuilding those routes.
concept.observation: Try every possible last coin, and keep only the smallest coin count for each amount. An unreachable amount cannot supply a route.
approach: Begin with the fact that amount zero needs no coins.
Solve amounts from small to large. For each amount, try removing one allowed final coin.
Add one coin to the best known answer for the remaining amount, and keep the cheapest valid choice.
If no choice reaches the requested amount, report that it is impossible.
concept.correctness: Every nonempty collection of coins has a final coin. Remove that coin and a smaller amount remains. If that smaller part could be made with fewer coins, replacing it would also improve the whole collection. Therefore an optimal answer can always use an optimal answer for its remaining amount. Comparing every possible final coin includes the final coin of an optimal collection, so the cheapest candidate is exact.

complexity.explanation: For every amount from zero to the target, compare every denomination. Work grows with the target amount multiplied by the number of denominations. Remember one best count per amount. This measures the amount itself, not merely the number of digits used to write it.

pitfalls: Largest-coin-first fails for arbitrary denominations, as 4 + 1 + 1 versus 3 + 3 shows.
Impossible smaller amounts must stay separate from valid coin counts.

illustrations.prompt: Use case: scientific-educational. A polished wide dark-background conceptual illustration for the Coin Change algorithm for beginners. Mathematical visual lecture aesthetics: charcoal-black, cyan, lime, warm ivory, spacious and restrained. Depict two alternative coin compositions reaching exactly the same amount six: top path a coin marked 4 followed by two coins each marked 1, bottom path two coins each marked 3. The top path has three coins; the bottom path has two coins and is illuminated lime. Coins may repeat. Thin arcs suggest routes meeting at one goal. Show only exact labels '4 + 1 + 1 = 6', '3 + 3 = 6', '3 coins', '2 coins'. Concept: the biggest coin can lead to more coins; compare the total number, not denomination size. No code, programming variables, UI controls, pseudo-code, extra denominations, logos, watermark, or untrue arithmetic. Wide illustration, not a screenshot.

scenes.title: The destination is six
scenes.narration: Our denominations are 1, 3, and 4. Each may be used repeatedly. We want the number of coins to be as small as possible.
scenes.decision: Compare counts of coins, not the value of the largest coin.

scenes.title: The tempting shortcut fails
scenes.narration: Taking 4 first leaves 2, which takes two 1s. That is three coins. Taking 3 and 3 uses only two.
scenes.decision: A local choice based on coin size does not guarantee the smallest total count.

scenes.title: Look at the final move
scenes.narration: A last coin worth 3 must follow a route to amount 3. One more coin extends that route to amount 6.
scenes.decision: A positive coin always refers to a smaller amount, whose best answer can already be known.

scenes.title: Build the smaller answers
scenes.narration: Amounts 0 through 5 have best counts 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, and 2. These answers are reused rather than solved again.
scenes.decision: Different ways to reach the same amount need only compete for its cheapest count.

scenes.title: Compare all routes to six
scenes.narration: A final 1 follows amount 5: three coins total. A final 3 follows amount 3: two coins. A final 4 follows amount 2: three coins.
scenes.decision: Choose the least count among every valid final move.

scenes.title: The winning route
scenes.narration: The minimum is two coins, both worth 3. Their values add to 6.
scenes.decision: The answer counts coins; it is not the amount or a list of chosen denominations.

scenes.title: Why the comparison is complete
scenes.narration: Every way of making 6 ends in a 1, a 3, or a 4. All three possibilities were compared.
scenes.decision: The best smaller answer plus that final coin is at least as good as any more expensive smaller route.

scenes.title: Zero is the starting destination
scenes.narration: Boundary example: amount zero is already reached before taking any coin. Its answer is zero, even when no positive target is reachable.
scenes.decision: A real zero-coin answer provides the base from which all valid routes grow.
